extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing MPEP §2106.04)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying whether patent claim limitations recite an 'abstract idea' under the Alice/Mayo framework (MPEP §2106.04), including enumerated groupings and examiner procedures for proceeding to Step 2A Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure to determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea (Step 2A Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should (1) identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determine whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the identified limitation(s) falls within at least one grouping, conclude the claim recites an abstract idea in Step 2A Prong One and proceed to Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (see MPEP §2106.04(d)). If the identified limitation(s) do not fall within any grouping, conclude the claim does not recite an abstract idea (eligible at Step 2A Prong One, Pathway B), except in the rare circumstances discussed in MPEP §2106.04(a)(3). If the claim recites another judicial exception (e.g., law of nature or natural phenomenon), follow the guidance in MPEP §§2106.04(b) and 2106.04(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated abstract idea groupings (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office groups abstract ideas into enumerated categories to guide examiners: (1) Mathematical concepts; (2) Certain methods of organizing human activity; and (3) Mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grouping-based approach shifts examiners from relying on individual cases to applying a broad body of precedent across technologies and claim types. Groupings are rooted in Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent. Groupings are not mutually exclusive; a limitation may fall within multiple groupings and examiners should identify at least one, preferably all applicable groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concepts (grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined as mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit decisions have repeatedly characterized mathematical relationships/formulas/calculations as abstract ideas. When assessing, consider whether the claim recites the mathematical concept itself, or merely limitations based on or involving a mathematical concept. A limitation merely based on or involving a mathematical concept may not fall into this grouping if the concept itself is not recited in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: A relationship between variables or numbers that can be expressed in words or mathematical symbols (e.g., pressure = F/A; Arrhenius relationship between reaction rate and temperature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include relationships expressed as formulas or described in words (e.g., directional radio activity vs. antenna arrangement). If the claim recites such relationships, it is an instance of the mathematical concepts grouping per MPEP §2106.04(a)(2)(I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formulas or equations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting a numerical formula or equation (or textual equivalent that is a replacement for a formula) is considered to fall within the mathematical concepts grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual descriptions like 'determining a ratio of A to B' or 'calculating the force by multiplying mass by acceleration' are treated as formulas. Examples include Arrhenius, conversion formulas (binary-coded decimal to pure binary), alarm-limit formulas, and hedging formulas cited in precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite mathematical operations or acts of calculating (e.g., multiplication, exponentiation, statistical analyses) are within the mathematical concepts grouping when, under the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification, they encompass a mathematical calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no single trigger word; terms like 'determining' or 'performing' may indicate calculations if the broad interpretation encompasses mathematical methods. Examples include resampled statistical analyses, alarm-limit computations, coordinate conversions, and insurance-policy calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain methods of organizing human activity (grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to fundamental economic principles/practices, commercial or legal interactions, and managing personal behavior/relationships or interactions between people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grouping is limited ('certain' methods) and should not be expanded beyond the enumerated sub-groupings except in rare circumstances (see MPEP §2106.04(a)(3)). The activity may involve one person or multiple people, and activity between a person and a computer can fall within the grouping. The number of people involved is not dispositive; determination depends on whether the activity itself falls within a sub-grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices or principles (subgroup)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes concepts relating to economy and commerce such as hedging, insurance, and mitigating risks; can include new methods that nonetheless constitute fundamental economic practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'fundamental' does not require the practice to be old or well-known; novel price-optimization or wagering rules have been found to be 'fundamental.' Examples from case law: hedging (Bilski), intermediated settlement (Alice), managing stable-value life insurance policy calculations (Bancorp). Other examples: mitigating settlement risk, offer-based price optimization, local processing of payments for remotely purchased goods, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions (subgroup)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, and business relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims reciting contractual relationships or transaction guarantees (e.g., transaction performance guaranty in buySAFE v. Google) are examples of this subgroup. Such commercial/legal interactions may be treated as abstract ideas when they recite those types of interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing personal behavior or relationships / interactions between people (subgroup)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts that manage a person's behavior, relationships, or interactions between people, including social activities, teaching, and following rules or instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This subgroup can encompass activities involving interactions with computers (e.g., anonymous loan shopping via mobile phone) if the activity itself falls within the subgroup. Not all human-activity methods fall here; e.g., a defined set of steps for combining ingredients into a drug formulation is not a 'method of organizing human activity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes (grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts performed in the human mind, including observation, evaluation, judgment, and opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely recite concepts that can be performed mentally are in this grouping. When a claimed limitation maps to such mental processes, it may be treated as an abstract idea under MPEP §2106.04(a)(2)(III).

rubrics_metrics.name: Groupings not mutually exclusive; identify multiple groupings when applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Some claims recite limitations that fall within more than one grouping or sub-grouping (e.g., a claim performing mathematical calculations using a formula that could be performed in the human mind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify at least one abstract-idea grouping, but preferably identify all groupings to the extent possible if a limitation falls within multiple groupings, and then proceed with Step 2A Prong Two analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of claims that do not recite abstract ideas (non-limiting hypotheticals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative claim types that do not themselves set forth or describe an abstract idea and therefore are eligible at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting examples provided: (i) a printer with belt, roller, printhead and ink cartridge; (ii) a washing machine with tub, drive motor, controller and housing; (iii) an earring with sensor and memory for glucose measurements; (iv) a method for sequencing BRCA1 gene sequences (PCR + sequencing); (v) a method for loading BIOS into a local computer system from remote memory and transferring control to BIOS; (vi) a GUI icon rearrangement method based on amount of use (processor tracking memory allocated over time and moving icons); (vii) a method of training a neural network for facial detection using staged training sets and transformed images. These examples illustrate claims that may be based on or involve abstract ideas but do not themselves recite an abstract idea.
